newsitem.title: BRAZIL: CVRD seen giving Brazil reserves $2.0 bln boost.
newsitem.headline: CVRD seen giving Brazil reserves $2.0 bln boost.

text.p: The $2.0 billion expected to flow into Brazil this month to help finance the purchase of state mining concern CVRD will pad foreign reserves and alleviate some current account worries, analysts said.

"This was widely expected, but it is certainly good news. These dollar flows are welcome and will come at a time when reserves seem to be in danger because of the widening current account gap," said Marcelo Carvalho, chief economist for J.P. Morgan in Brazil.
Brazilian reserves fell by about $2.0 billion last month to about $56 billion, with most of the money going toward interest and amortization payments on foreign debt.
Also, the nation's relentless trade deficit has increasingly pressured the current account over the past six months.
As evidence of growing official concern over reserve levels and the current account, the Central Bank late last month cut taxes foreign investors pay on short-term investments.
The move was widely viewed as a bid to beef up reserves and prevent them from falling below the $58 billion level.

At Tuesday's auction in Rio de Janeiro, a group led by Brazilian steelmaker CSN paid 3.33 billion reais ($3.15 billion) for a 41.7 percent stake in CVRD. About $2.0 billion of that, including a $1.2 billion loan from NationsBank, was expected to come from abroad.
It was the first of three phases in the government's CVRD privatization plan.
Also this year, the government is expected to sell five percent of its shares to CVRD employees and then carry out a global offering of its remaining shares.
All told, the CVRD privatization should raise $5.0 billion for the federal government, with roughly two-thirds of that coming from financing abroad.
Brazil needs about $50 billion in external financing this year to cover an estimated $30-$35 billion current account gap and foreign debt amortization payments.
Roughly half of that is expected to come in the form of Eurobonds, commercial paper, bank loans and trade finance, said Marcelo Allain, chief economist at BMC bank in Brazil.
Foreign direct investment, including the CVRD sale and other privatizations, is expected to account for $15 billion. Another $15 billion will come in the form of portfolio investment, Allain said.
